title: Divine wisdom, knowledge and faith
source_text: Οὐκοῦν κατὰ ταῦτα ἡ μέν τις θεία σοφία ἐστὶν, ἡ δ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνη. καὶ ἡ μὲν ἀνθρωπίνη ἐστὶν ἡ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς λεγομένη „σοφία τοῦ κόσμου“. ἥτις ἐστὶ „μωρία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ“· ἡ δὲ θεία καὶ ἑτέρα παρὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην, εἴπερ ἐστὶ θεία, χάριτι θεοῦ δωρουμένου αὐτὴν τοῖς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιτηδείους πρὸς παραδοχὴν αὐτῆς κατασκευάσασι παραγίνεται, καὶ μάλιστα τοῖς ἐκ τοῦ ἐγνωκέναι τὴν διαφορὰν ἑκατέρας σοφίας πρὸς τὴν ἑτέραν ἐν ταῖς πρὸς θεὸν εὐχαῖς λέγουσι· „κἂν γάρ τις τέλειος ἐν υἱοῖς ἀνθρώπων, τῆς ἀπὸ σοῦ σοφίας ἀπούσης εἰς οὐδὲν λογισθήσεται.“ καὶ γυμνάσιον μέν φαμεν εἶναι τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην σοφίαν, τέλος δὲ τὴν θείαν· ἥτις καὶ „στερεὰ“ λέγεται τῆς ψυχῆς εἶναι „τροφὴ“ παρὰ τῷ φήσαντι· „τελείων δέ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφὴ, τῶν διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἐχόντων πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ.“ καὶ ἀρχαία μὲν ἀληθῶς ἐστιν ἥδε ἡ δόξα. οὐχ, ὡς οἴεται δὲ Κέλσος, τῆς περὶ αὐτῶν ἀρχαιότητος εἰς Ἡράκλειτον καὶ Πλάτωνα ἀναφερομένης. ἀνωτέρω γὰρ τούτων οἱ προφῆται διέστειλαν τὸ περὶ ἑκατέρας σοφίας· ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος εἰπεῖν ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων τοῦ Δαυῒδ τὸ περὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν θείαν σοφίαν σοφοῦ λεγόμενον, ὅστις „οὐκ ὄψεται καταφθορὰν,“ φησὶν, „ὅταν ἴδῃ σοφοὺς ἀποθνῄσκοντας.“ ἡ θεία τοίνυν σοφία, ἑτέρα οὖσα τῆς πίστεως, πρῶτόν ἐστι τῶν καλουμένων· „χαρισμάτων“ τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ μετ᾿ ἐκείνην δεύτερον τοῖς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπισταμένοις ἡ καλουμένη γνῶσις, καὶ τρίτον, ἐπεὶ σῴζεσθαι χρὴ καὶ τοὺς ἁπλουστέρους προσιόντας κατὰ δύναμιν τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ, ἡ πίστις. διὸ λέγεται παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ· „ᾧ μὲν γὰρ διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος δίδοται λόγος σοφίας, ἄλλῳ δὲ λόγος γνώσεως κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, ἑτέρῳ δὲ πίστις ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι.“ διόπερ οὐ τοὺς τυχόντας εὕροις ἂν μετειληφότας τῆς θείας σοφίας ἀλλὰ τοὺς ὑπερέχοντας καὶ διαφέροντας πάντων τῶν χριστιανισμῷ προσεχόντων, οὐδὲ τοῖς ἀπαιδευτοτάτοις ἢ ἀνδραπόδοις ἢ ἀμαθεστάτοις διέξεισί τις τὰ περὶ τῆς θείας σοφίας.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore (οὐκοῦν) according to these, one is a certain divine (θεία) wisdom, the other human (ἀνθρωπίνη). And the human is that called among us 'wisdom of the world (σοφία τοῦ κόσμου)', which is 'foolishness (μωρία) with God'; but the divine, also other than (ἑτέρα παρά) the human, if indeed it is divine, comes (παραγίνεται) by grace (χάριτι) of God giving it as a gift (δωρουμένου) to those who have prepared (κατασκευάσασι) themselves fit (ἐπιτηδείους) for its reception (παραδοχή), and especially to those who, from having known (ἐγνωκέναι) the difference (διαφορά) of each wisdom against the other, say in their prayers (εὐχαί) to God: 'for even if someone be perfect (τέλειος) among sons of men, the wisdom from you being absent (ἀπούσης), he will be reckoned (λογισθήσεται) as nothing.' And we say human wisdom is an exercise/training ground (γυμνάσιον) of the soul, but the divine the end (τέλος); which is also called 'solid (στερεά) food (τροφή)' of the soul by the one who said: 'of the perfect/mature (τέλειοι) is the solid food, of those having through habit (ἕξις) the sense-organs (αἰσθητήρια) trained (γεγυμνασμένα) for discernment (διάκρισις) of good and evil.' And ancient (ἀρχαία) truly is this opinion (δόξα), not, as Celsus thinks, the antiquity (ἀρχαιότης) about them going back (ἀναφερομένης) to Heraclitus and Plato. For higher/earlier than these the prophets distinguished (διέστειλαν) the matter of each wisdom; it suffices for the present to say from the words of David what is said about the one wise according to divine wisdom, who 'will not see corruption (καταφθορά),' he says, 'when he sees wise men dying.' The divine wisdom then, being other than faith (πίστις), is first of the so-called 'gifts (χαρίσματα)' of God, and after it second, for/in the view of those who know how to be exact (ἀκριβοῦν) about such things, the so-called knowledge (γνῶσις), and third, since even the simpler (ἁπλούστεροι) who approach godliness (θεοσέβεια) according to ability must be saved (σῴζεσθαι), faith. Therefore it is said by Paul: 'for to one through the Spirit (πνεῦμα) is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit.' Therefore you would not find ordinary people (οἱ τυχόντες) having shared (μετειληφότας) in divine wisdom, but those surpassing (ὑπερέχοντας) and excelling (διαφέροντας) all who adhere (προσεχόντων) to Christianity (χριστιανισμός), nor does anyone go through (διέξεισι) the things of divine wisdom to the most uneducated (ἀπαιδευτότατοι) or slaves (ἀνδράποδα) or most ignorant (ἀμαθέστατοι).
pass_b_english: According to these passages, then, there is a divine wisdom and a human one. The human is what we call “the wisdom of the world,” which is “foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). But the divine, which differs from the human, if it is indeed divine, comes by the grace of God, who gives it to those who have made themselves fit to receive it, and above all to those who know how each wisdom differs from the other and therefore say in their prayers to God: “For even if one is perfect among the sons of men, yet if the wisdom that comes from you is absent, he will be counted as nothing” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:6).

We say that human wisdom is a training ground for the soul, and divine wisdom its goal. Divine wisdom is also called the “solid food” of the soul by the one who said: “But solid food is for the mature, for those whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:14).

This view is truly ancient, but its antiquity does not go back, as Celsus thinks, to Heraclitus and Plato. For before them the prophets drew the distinction between the two kinds of wisdom. For the present it is enough to quote from the words of David what is said of the man who is wise with divine wisdom: he “will not see corruption,” David says, “when he sees the wise dying” (Psalm 49:9–10).

Divine wisdom, then, which is different from faith, is the first of what are called the “gifts” of God (1 Corinthians 12:4). After it, second, for those who know how to be exact in such matters, comes what is called knowledge; and third, since the simpler people too, who come to godliness as best they can, must be saved, comes faith. That is why Paul says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). So you would find that it is not ordinary people who have a share in divine wisdom, but those who rise above and excel all who hold to Christianity; nor does anyone expound the matters of divine wisdom to the most uneducated, or to slaves, or to the most ignorant.

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: ‘will not see corruption when he sees the wise dying’ is LXX Psalm 48:10–11 = English Psalm 49:9–10 (Rahlfs 48:10 ends at καταφθοράν, 48:11 begins ὅταν ἴδῃ). In the psalm the subject is the man trusting in wealth; Origen applies the words to the one wise with divine wisdom, and the English follows Origen’s application. ‘Gifts’ (χαρισμάτων) is cited to 1 Corinthians 12:4 as the place Paul introduces the gifts, since the quotation that follows is 1 Corinthians 12:8–9. τοῖς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπισταμένοις is ambiguous: either ‘in the reckoning of those who know how to be exact about such things’ or ‘for those who know how to be exact’ (as the recipients of knowledge); the English ‘for those who know how to be exact in such matters’ keeps the ambiguity. The final three terms (‘most uneducated’, ‘slaves’, ‘most ignorant’) are Celsus’s own labels for Christian converts, taken up again at the start of the next chapter; they are not quoted here because the Greek does not attribute them in this sentence. Hebrews 5:14: τέλειοι rendered ‘mature’; Origen plays on γυμνάσιον / γεγυμνασμένα (‘training ground’ / ‘trained’) and on τέλος / τέλειοι (‘goal’ / ‘mature’), which English cannot fully keep.
Restored omitted 'For' (γάρ) in 'For before them the prophets drew the distinction'
